articles.title: California votes to give record $8.4 billion to medical research
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03635-6The cash infusion, earmarked for immunology studies, is the largest ever for science authorized by a US public vote — but it has drawn criticism.
articles.content:
Students, researchers and others at the University of California, Los Angeles, have protested over cuts to science funding made by the administration of US President Donald Trump during the past two years.Credit: Robyn Beck/AFP via Getty

Voters in California have approved US$8.4 billion in funding for immunology research — the largest ever infusion of cash for science authorized by a public vote in US history.

The funding proposal, known as Proposition 38, appeared on the ballot for voters in California in last week’s US mid-term elections, but it has taken nearly a week for officials to count enough ballots to declare it a success. The state government will pay for the research — which aims to find treatments that harness or re-engineer the body’s immune system to fight illnesses such as cancer and Alzheimer’s disease — by selling state government bonds. (This is unusual for science funding. Bonds are typically reserved to pay for infrastructure projects such as road construction and require the state to pay back its debt with interest.)

‘Historic change’: what the 2026 US mid-term election results mean for science

Supporters of the proposal say that the funding will provide stability for researchers in California, who have been affected by political turmoil. The administration of US President Donald Trump has pushed for massive cuts to science funding; put political appointees in charge of grant decisions at federal science agencies such as the US National Institutes of Health; and forced policy change at US universities that receive federal funding, including those in California.

The $8.4 billion “is an advantage to California that is unprecedented”, says Antoni Ribas, a cancer researcher and physician at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), who supported Proposition 38. It will make the state “even more of a global hub for immunology research”.

But the proposal has sparked debate. That’s because it calls for about half of the funding to be given directly to research institutes — and the only institute that matches the criteria called for in the proposal is one co-founded by Gary Michelson, a billionaire medical-device inventor. He wrote the proposition and donated about $45 million of his own funds to get it placed on the ballot and to campaign for its passage.

“I feel like the voters have been taken advantage of,” says Sarah Hill, a political scientist at California State University in Fullerton, who tracks the state’s ballot measures. Michelson did not respond to Nature’s request for comment before this story was published, but has said elsewhere that he will not personally profit from the bond revenue.

State funding

In California, citizens can place proposed laws directly on the election ballot by collecting hundreds of thousands of voter signatures.

The state has funded scientific research through this process before. In 2004, after then president George W. Bush restricted federal funding for human embryonic stem-cell research, voters in California approved a $3-billion bond to establish the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine, which they then voted to replenish with another $5.5 billion in 2020.

A campaign mailer encouraging California voters to support Proposition 38.Credit: Smith Collection/Gado/Getty

“The model works,” Ribas says. Immunologists have been making great strides with medicines such as personalized treatments called CAR-T therapies, which are revolutionizing care, he says. There has also been a flurry of research into developing vaccines, including the mRNA shots that have been the target of funding cuts by the Trump administration. Proposition 38 will ensure that such research can continue regardless of the political headwinds, Ribas adds.

Around $4 billion from Proposition 38 will fund grants for researchers at select public universities and non-profit institutes in California through a competitive review process. According to the proposal, any commercialized therapies developed through funded research must be sold at a 20% discount to people in California, with 10% of drug royalties returning to the state’s general fund.

This funding will support critical medical research with broad societal benefits, including treatments for cancer and Alzheimer's disease. The initiative provides stability for researchers amid federal funding cuts and promotes significant progress in health science with measurable impact on public well-being.

articles.title: Eating less protein could slow aging, review of 350 studies finds
articles.summary: A major review of more than 350 studies suggests that eating less protein could slow aging, improve metabolic health, and potentially extend lifespan, challenging the widespread belief that more protein is always better. Researchers warn that many sedentary adults may be consuming too much protein, while emphasizing that individual needs depend on age and physical activity.
articles.content:
Protein is everywhere these days. From breakfast cereals and coffee to bottled water, manufacturers are adding extra protein to an expanding range of everyday products. But while consumers are being encouraged to eat more of it, a major scientific review suggests that cutting back on protein could offer surprising benefits for health and longevity.

After examining more than 350 scientific papers, researchers found evidence that reducing protein intake may help slow biological aging, improve metabolism, and, under certain conditions, extend lifespan. The potential benefits appear to involve several processes that influence how the body uses energy, responds to nutrients, protects cells from damage, and maintains healthy cellular function.

The findings, published in the Cell Press journal Cell Press Blue, raise an important question about the growing enthusiasm for high-protein diets. Could many people be consuming far more protein than their bodies actually need?

"It's absolutely crystal clear that there are benefits of protein to muscle growth and exercise response of active individuals," says Dudley Lamming, the paper's corresponding author, of the University of Wisconsin-Madison. "But because most people are relatively sedentary, many people are likely consuming more protein than they actually need, which probably has negative health consequences."

Why Eating Less Protein Could Promote Longevity

Scientists have long understood that reducing calorie intake can extend lifespan in numerous organisms. Research has also linked calorie restriction to a lower risk of diseases associated with aging, including cancer. However, consistently eating fewer calories is challenging, making it difficult for many people to maintain such a diet over time.

An alternative approach has attracted increasing scientific interest: reducing protein without necessarily eating less food.

Experiments involving flies and rodents have demonstrated that limiting protein intake can increase lifespan even when total calorie consumption remains unchanged. This suggests that the benefits of dietary restriction may depend not only on how much food is consumed, but also on which nutrients make up that food.

Human research has produced encouraging findings as well. Several recent clinical trials have shown that people who reduce their protein intake can lose weight, decrease body fat, and improve fasting blood sugar levels, even when they consume more calories overall. Fasting blood sugar measures glucose in the bloodstream after a period without eating and is an important indicator of metabolic health.

These findings do not establish that protein restriction extends human lifespan, but they suggest that changing protein intake can influence processes associated with aging and disease.

The Debate Over How Much Protein We Really Need

The picture becomes more complicated when exercise and muscle health enter the equation.

Other studies have demonstrated that higher protein intake can support weight loss and help older adults preserve muscle mass, particularly when combined with physical activity. Maintaining muscle becomes increasingly important with age because muscle loss can contribute to weakness, reduced mobility, and a greater risk of falls.

Research highlighting these benefits helped motivate US authorities to revise dietary recommendations this year, encouraging daily protein consumption of 1.2-1.6 grams per kilogram of body weight (0.5-0.7 grams per pound). That represents nearly twice the previous recommended amount.

With protein consumption reaching new highs in the United States and older adults increasingly being advised to eat more, Lamming and a colleague examined decades of research to better understand the relationship between protein intake and aging.

Their analysis brought together findings from more than 350 papers, identifying several biological mechanisms that repeatedly appeared across studies. Together, these mechanisms suggest that lowering protein consumption may improve metabolic function, alter the way cells detect nutrients, limit cellular damage, and help preserve the processes that keep cells functioning properly.

A Hormone That May Help Explain Slower Aging

One particularly intriguing finding involves fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21), a hormone that becomes more abundant when dietary protein is limited.

FGF21 helps the body adjust to changes in nutrient availability and influences how energy is used. Higher levels of this hormone can increase energy expenditure, support healthier blood sugar regulation, and reduce inflammation.

These effects are especially interesting because metabolism and chronic inflammation are closely connected to aging. Over time, disruptions in these processes can contribute to conditions such as obesity, diabetes, and other age-related diseases.

Studies in mice have shown that animals with elevated FGF21 levels live longer than mice with normal levels. The lifespan benefit was particularly strong in males, suggesting that biological sex may influence how the body responds to this hormone.

Researchers have also established that eating less protein increases FGF21 levels in humans. Whether this hormonal response produces the same longevity benefits seen in mice remains an important unanswered question.

How Certain Amino Acids Could Influence Aging

The amount of protein someone eats may not be the only factor that matters. The types of amino acids that make up that protein could also play an important role.

Amino acids are the building blocks the body uses to produce proteins, which are essential for maintaining muscles, repairing tissues, and carrying out countless cellular functions. Beyond these basic roles, certain amino acids also act as signals that influence metabolism and cellular growth.

The review identifies three amino acids that appear especially important: methionine, isoleucine, and valine.

Research suggests that excessive intake of these amino acids can stimulate biological pathways that encourage growth. Although growth-related processes are essential for normal development and tissue repair, excessive or prolonged activation of certain pathways may contribute to obesity, inflammation, and other conditions associated with aging.

Limiting specific amino acids could therefore produce some of the benefits observed in protein-restricted diets. This possibility has attracted attention because it suggests that the relationship between protein and longevity may be more complicated than simply eating more or less of a single nutrient.

"These studies show that the amount of protein sedentary people are eating today may have negative health consequences, at least at the population level," Lamming says.

Why Exercise Could Change the Effects of Protein

The researchers emphasize that protein requirements are not the same for everyone.

Pregnant women, for example, need additional protein to support fetal development, while some older adults require higher amounts to help maintain muscle and physical function. People who exercise regularly may also benefit from greater protein consumption because their muscles use those nutrients to recover, repair tissue, and adapt to training.

For many adults who spend most of their day sitting, however, adding protein to everyday foods may offer little additional benefit.

Lamming points out that athletes frequently consume large amounts of protein without developing the metabolic diseases sometimes associated with protein-rich diets. One possible explanation is that physical activity changes how the body handles those nutrients.

Regular exercise stimulates muscle growth and repair, potentially allowing the body to put additional protein to productive use while reducing some of the harmful metabolic effects associated with high protein intake.

This distinction may help explain why studies sometimes reach seemingly contradictory conclusions about protein. A diet that benefits someone who exercises intensely may not be ideal for someone with a largely sedentary lifestyle.

Rather than recommending the same amount of protein for everyone, the researchers argue that dietary advice should better reflect individual circumstances, especially physical activity levels and age.

"Recent recommendations have encouraged people to eat more protein, but they've also encouraged people to exercise more," Lamming says. "We probably need to personalize protein recommendations based not just on age, but also on how physically active people are."

The findings challenge the assumption that adding more protein automatically leads to better health. Although protein remains essential, the growing body of longevity research suggests that for some people, consuming less may offer benefits that have been overlooked in the rush toward protein-rich foods.

The work was supported by the National Institute on Aging, the Wisconsin Partnership Program, and the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

articles.title: World News in Brief: Ending cholera by 2030 ‘within reach’, Haiti displacement and hunger, US human rights review rescheduled
articles.summary: Ending cholera as a public health threat by 2030 is within reach, as every cholera death can be prevented with tools that already exist, the World Health Organization (WHO) said on Tuesday.
articles.content:
Last year was the deadliest for cholera since 1999, with almost 7,900 deaths, Dr. Lorenzo Pezzoli, WHO lead for epidemic-prone bacterial diseases, told journalists in Geneva.

Tweet URL

Most of the deaths happened on a community level, before patients could access healthcare.

Nearly 90 per cent of deaths in Africa

Fatalities dipped down in the first nine months of 2026, but more than 3,000 have still died of the preventable and treatable disease – nearly nine in ten of them in Africa.

Where there is clean water, basic sanitation and a nearby health centre, patients can recover, Dr. Pezzoli said. But in a crowded camp or a village cut off by conflict, cholera can turn deadly within hours, and El Niño could make matters worse, since both too much and too little water fuel the disease.

Most cases are currently being reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Yemen, Zambia, Nigeria, Somalia and Djibouti. WHO has already provided 71 million doses of cholera vaccine.

Sufficient clean water and sanitation facilities would end cholera for good, Dr. Pezzoli said – but not where conflict is raging.

Haiti: Thousands flee violence as hunger deepens

Armed violence continues to force people from their homes in Haiti’s West Department, UN Deputy Spokesperson Farhan Haq told journalists in New York on Tuesday.

Since late October, attacks in Arcahaie and Cabaret, northwest of Port-au-Prince, have displaced more than 5,900 people, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). Some 70 per cent are staying with host families, while the rest are sheltering in makeshift sites.

Meanwhile, hunger continues to deepen. Nearly six million people, more than half the population, face high levels of acute food insecurity, including nearly 1.9 million at emergency levels.

Acute malnutrition

The UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) estimates that more than a quarter of a million children aged six to 59 months are expected to suffer from acute malnutrition between June this year and May next year, including nearly 94,000 with severe acute malnutrition.

Humanitarians are assessing needs and assisting the hardest-hit families, but insecurity continues to hamper access, Mr. Haq said.

The $880 million humanitarian plan for Haiti is less than half funded, with $424 million received as the year draws to a close.

US human rights review rescheduled after ‘continued non-cooperation’

The UN Human Rights Council on Tuesday expressed regret at the “continued non-cooperation” of the United States with the universal periodic review (UPR) mechanism, after the Government declined to take part in its scheduled review for the second time.

Tweet URL

The US review had originally been set for 7 November 2025. After the country did not participate, it was rescheduled for Tuesday but the US failed to comply again.

Under the Universal Periodic Review, every Member State, whatever its size or influence, appears before its peers in Geneva about once every four and a half years.

Universal obligation

It presents a report on its human rights record, answers questions and receives recommendations from other countries.

In a decision adopted in Geneva, the council called on the US to “resume its cooperation with the universal periodic review mechanism” and rescheduled the review for its next Working Group session, from 18 to 29 January 2027.

The other States scheduled for review by the UPR Working Group during its current session (2-13 November 2026) are: Suriname, Greece, Samoa, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, Hungary, Papua New Guinea, Tajikistan, the United Republic of Tanzania, Antigua and Barbuda, Eswatini, Trinidad and Tobago, Thailand and Ireland.

**Impact** – C'est important car les décès dus au choléra surviennent surtout dans les endroits sans eau propre ni centres de santé. Si ces besoins de base sont assurés, les malades peuvent guérir rapidement. Le choléra se propage vite dans les zones surpeuplées ou en conflit, et des phénomènes climatiques comme El Niño peuvent aggraver la situation. Cette stratégie montre une voie claire pour sauver des milliers de vies, notamment en Afrique dans des pays comme la République démocratique du Congo et le Nigeria.

**Prochaine étape** – Pour éliminer le choléra définitivement, il faut renforcer les efforts pour fournir de l'eau propre, un meilleur assainissement et des vaccins, surtout dans les zones touchées par les conflits ou les catastrophes naturelles. Le soutien continu des gouvernements et des organisations sera essentiel pour atteindre l'objectif 2030.

**En une phrase** – Grâce aux vaccins, à l'eau propre et à l'assainissement, mettre fin aux décès dus au choléra d'ici 2030 est un objectif réaliste selon l'OMS.
articles.personality_title_es: La eliminación del cólera para 2030 está al alcance, dice la OMS
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El cólera es una enfermedad que causa diarrea fuerte y deshidratación, y puede ser mortal sin tratamiento. El año pasado, casi 7,900 personas murieron por cólera, principalmente en África, donde es difícil acceder a agua limpia y atención médica.

**Qué pasó** – La Organización Mundial de la Salud (OMS) anunció que eliminar el cólera como amenaza para la salud pública para 2030 es posible con las herramientas que ya existen. Estas incluyen vacunas, agua limpia, saneamiento y acceso a servicios de salud. La OMS ha entregado 71 millones de dosis de vacuna contra el cólera.

**Impacto** – Esto es importante porque la mayoría de las muertes por cólera ocurren en lugares sin agua limpia ni centros de salud cercanos. Si estas necesidades básicas se cumplen, las personas pueden recuperarse rápidamente. El cólera se puede propagar rápido en campamentos llenos de gente o en zonas de conflicto, y fenómenos como El Niño pueden empeorar la situación. Este enfoque ofrece un camino claro para salvar miles de vidas, especialmente en países africanos como la República Democrática del Congo y Nigeria.

**Próximo paso** – Para eliminar el cólera definitivamente, se deben aumentar los esfuerzos para proporcionar agua limpia, mejorar el saneamiento y aplicar vacunas, especialmente en áreas afectadas por conflictos o desastres naturales. El apoyo continuo de gobiernos y organizaciones será clave para lograr la meta de 2030.

**Resumen en una frase** – Con vacunas y mejor agua y saneamiento, acabar con las muertes por cólera para 2030 es una meta realista según la OMS.
